papers.title: The Independent and Combined Effects of Mindfulness Meditation and Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation on Central Pain Processing in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The Pain Relief for OsteoArthritis through Combined Treatment (PROACT) was a proof-of-principle mechanistic randomized controlled trial to examine the effects of Breathing and Attention Training (BAT), and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on pain modulatory balance, pain-related brain function, and clinical pain in middle-aged to older adults with knee osteoarthritis (OA). METHODS: Participants completed baseline health screening, clinical knee pain assessment, quantitative sensory testing (QST), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in response to mechanical pain evocation of the index knee. They were randomized to receive concurrent sham BAT/sham tDCS, active BAT/sham tDCS, sham BAT/active tDCS or active BAT/active tDCS. Participants completed 20-minute interventions for five consecutive days. After, participants repeated the clinical knee pain assessment, QST, and fMRI. RESULTS: Adjusted analyses of 226 completers revealed no significant main effects of treatment on clinical pain or pain modulatory balance. However, average pain-evoked cerebral blood flow across pain-related regions of interest was significantly lower for active tDCS (-3.14 [CI:-4.83- -1.45]) vs. sham tDCS (-0.51 [CI:-2.19-1.17]), though this finding did not survive multiple correction. Pre-planned follow-up comparisons revealed that the active BAT/active tDCS group showed lower post-intervention pain-evoked cerebral blood flow than the sham BAT/sham tDCS group. CONCLUSIONS: The PROACT study found that mindfulness meditation in combination with tDCS may reduce pain-evoked cerebral blood flow in adults with knee OA. Future research is needed to determine if a longer duration of exposure to the combined active BAT/active tDCS treatment beneficially influences pain modulatory balance and clinical knee pain in this population.

papers.title: Parenting for Families at Risk: A Systematic Review of the Role of Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Skills Training for Maltreatment Prevention.
papers.abstract: Parents with histories of psychopathology, trauma, and systemic stressors are at elevated risk for emotion dysregulation, a modifiable driver of child maltreatment. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) offers transdiagnostic skills that may reduce this risk; however, the evidence for DBT-informed parenting interventions has not been synthesized. This Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses-guided systematic review examined how such interventions are designed, implemented, and evaluated. PubMed, PsycINFO, and MEDLINE were searched from inception to February 2026. Eligible studies were empirical evaluations of DBT-informed parenting programmes for caregivers of children, reporting parent, parenting, or child outcomes; case studies and non-empirical reports were excluded. Of 109 full texts screened, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies were coded for intervention characteristics, DBT module coverage (including the use of behaviour chain analysis [BCA], risk of bias (ROBINS-I), and parent and parenting outcomes. Interventions were typically brief (6-14 weeks), group-based, and clinician-delivered; all included mindfulness, and most included emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness. Notably, only one study explicitly reported utilizing BCA. Caregivers showed reductions in emotion dysregulation, depression, anxiety, and parenting stress, alongside decreases in coercive or harsh parenting and gains in validation, effective discipline, and parent-child communication. Evidence was derived primarily from small, uncontrolled pilots; risk of bias was commonly rated as serious, and the overall certainty of evidence was low. Rigorous controlled trials with diverse caregivers are needed. DBT-informed parenting programmes show promise for reducing risk factors associated with maltreatment.
